newsitem.title: USA: Key evidence admitted into Oklahoma bombing case.
newsitem.headline: Key evidence admitted into Oklahoma bombing case.

text.p: Government prosecutors on Monday successfully introduced a key piece of evidence -- the telephone calling card they claim alleged bomber Timothy McVeigh used to find chemicals needed to make the bomb that destroyed the Oklahoma City federal building.
Despite objections from McVeigh's attorneys, Federal Judge Richard Matsch allowed the pre-paid telephone calling card issued by a far right-wing magazine, Spotlight, to be entered into evidence.
The card was found three days after the bombing during a room by room search of the Herington, Kansas, home of McVeigh's alleged co-conspirator Terry Nichols, who will be tried separately later.

Prosecutors, who are systematically laying down a blanket of circumstantial evidence to tie the 29-year-old McVeigh to the bombing that killed 168 people, say the calling card was used by McVeigh and Nichols in late 1994 to accumulate the materials used in the bombing.

Also introduced into evidence were four white plastic barrels that were found in the garage of Nichols' home along with $5,200 in cash and an undisclosed number of gold coins. The government alleges that the barrels were similar to the kind used by McVeigh to make the explosive that destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995.
Last week the government presented an array of witnesses that McVeigh had allegedly contacted to buy a detonator card as well as racing fuel and ammonium nitrate fertiliser to make the massive bomb.
The lead prosecutor, Joseph Hartzler, on Monday confirmed news reports that he will quit the case after the McVeigh trial is completed, leaving the prosecution of Nichols up to someone else.
"I think I'll keep my feelings to myself," Hartzler told Reuters when asked how he feels about not going on to try Nichols.

Hartzler is leaving so he can spend more time with his family in Springfield, Ill., where he is an assistant U.S. attorney, said Justice Department spokeswoman Leesa Brown. He made only a two-year commitment to Attorney General Janet Reno, who picked him in May, 1995, to oversee the bombing case, Brown added.
Although Hartzler uses a wheelchair because he has multiple sclerosis, the decision to quit "has nothing to do with Joe's health," Brown said.
